\begin{definition}[Boolean circuit gate types]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate}

\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{

  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p006-b003
}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate}
\leanok
A circuit gate is either a logical AND gate or a logical OR gate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dual of a Boolean gate]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.dual}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b005}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.dual}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate}
The dual of an AND gate is an OR gate, and the dual of an OR gate is an AND gate.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Dual of an AND gate]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_and}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_and}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate.dual}
\difficulty{1}
The dual of a logical AND gate is a logical OR gate.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dual of an OR gate]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_or}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_or}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate.dual}
\difficulty{1}
The dual of a logical OR gate is a logical AND gate.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Involution of gate duality]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_dual}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.dual_dual}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate, FABL.CircuitGate.dual}
\difficulty{4}
For either a logical AND gate or a logical OR gate, taking the dual twice returns the
original gate.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Evaluation of a term by a gate]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.evalTerm}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p093-b004}
\statementsource{goldreich-approximation-method}{
  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p006-b001,
  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p006-b002,
  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p006-b003
}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.evalTerm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula.clauseEval, FABL.CircuitGate, FABL.DNFTerm, FABL.DNFTerm.eval, FABL.Sign}
Let a term on $n$ Boolean coordinates be given, together with an input $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$.
Evaluating the term with an AND gate gives the term's conjunction evaluation, while
evaluating it with an OR gate gives the clause evaluation of the same literals.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Evaluation of a finite set of inputs]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p093-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b004
}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate, FABL.Sign}
Let $m$ be a nonnegative integer, assign a sign in $\{-1,1\}$ to each of $m$ inputs, and
choose a finite set $I$ of input indices. The AND gate returns $-1$ exactly when every
input in $I$ has value $-1$, and otherwise returns $1$; the OR gate returns $-1$ exactly
when some input in $I$ has value $-1$, and otherwise returns $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of AND evaluation]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset_and_eq_neg_one_iff}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset_and_eq_neg_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset, FABL.Sign}
\difficulty{1}
Let $m$ be a natural number, let $m$ signs in $\{ -1,1 \}$ be given, and choose any
subset of their indices. The AND gate applied to the chosen signs equals $-1$ if and
only if every chosen sign equals $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[OR gate evaluation criterion]
\lean{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset_or_eq_neg_one_iff}
\label{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset_or_eq_neg_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset, FABL.Sign}
\difficulty{1}
Let $m$ be a nonnegative integer, let $v:\text{Fin}(m)\to\{\pm1\}$ be a sign assignment,
and let $S\subseteq\text{Fin}(m)$. The OR gate evaluates to $-1$ on $S$ exactly when
some index in $S$ has assigned value $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Recursive circuit tail]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p103-b002}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail}
\leanok
For each nonnegative integer $m$, a circuit tail with $m$ available inputs is either an
output layer specified by a finite set of input indices, or a non-output layer specified
by a list of finite sets of input indices, followed by a circuit tail whose number of
available inputs equals the length of that list.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Number of circuit layers]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail.layerCount}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p103-b002}
\statementsource{goldreich-approximation-method}{
  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p004-b004,
  pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p005-b002
}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail.layerCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitTail}
The layer count of a circuit tail is $1$ for an output layer, and is one plus the layer
count of the remaining tail for a non-output layer.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Every circuit tail has a layer]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail.one_le_layerCount}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail.one_le_layerCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitTail, FABL.CircuitTail.layerCount}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $m$ and every circuit tail with $m$ inputs, the number of
layers is at least $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A single layer is the output layer]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail.eq_output_of_layerCount_eq_one}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail.eq_output_of_layerCount_eq_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitTail, FABL.CircuitTail.layerCount, FABL.CircuitTail.one_le_layerCount}
\difficulty{4}
Let a circuit tail have layer count equal to $1$. Then it is an output layer, specified
by some finite set of incoming wires.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Number of internal nodes]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail.internalNodeCount}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p104-b001}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail.internalNodeCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitTail}
The internal node count of an output layer is $0$. For a non-output layer, it is the
number of gates in that layer plus the internal node count of the remaining tail.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Evaluation of a circuit tail]
\lean{FABL.CircuitTail.eval}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p103-b002}
\label{FABL.CircuitTail.eval}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate, FABL.CircuitGate.dual, FABL.CircuitGate.evalFinset, FABL.CircuitTail, FABL.Sign}
Let a circuit tail have $m$ available inputs, assign a sign in $\{-1,1\}$ to each input,
and choose an initial gate type, AND or OR. For an output layer, evaluate its designated
inputs using that gate. For a non-output layer, evaluate each gate in the layer on its
designated inputs, then evaluate the remaining tail on those gate outputs using the dual
gate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Depth circuit structure]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}

\label{FABL.DepthCircuit}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CircuitGate, FABL.CircuitTail, FABL.DNFTerm}
A depth circuit on $n$ Boolean coordinates consists of a gate type shared by all gates
in the first layer, a list of first-layer gates each specified by a term on those
coordinates, and a circuit tail whose number of available inputs is the number of gates
in the first layer.
\end{definition}

\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.width_ofDNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DNFFormula, FABL.DNFFormula.width, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofDNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.width}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $\phi$ be a disjunctive normal form on $n$
coordinates, with terms having pairwise distinct literal coordinates. The width of the
circuit formed from these terms as its first layer of AND gates equals the width of
$\phi$.
\end{theorem}

\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofDNF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p093-b004}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofDNF}
\leanok

\begin{theorem}[Circuit representation of a DNF function]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction_ofDNF}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p093-b004}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction_ofDNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DNFFormula, FABL.DNFFormula.toBooleanFunction, FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofDNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofDNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction}
\difficulty{3}
For every DNF formula on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, the Boolean function computed by
the circuit formed from that formula is equal to the function represented by the
formula.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Circuit from a CNF formula]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch13-circuit-lowerbounds}{pdf-52929dbaa962-p002-b002}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p103-b002
}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula, FABL.DepthCircuit}
Given a conjunctive normal form formula on $n$ variables, form a depth circuit whose
first layer consists of its clauses, with each clause represented by an OR gate, and
whose output layer takes all first-layer gates as inputs.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Depth of the CNF circuit]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.depth_ofCNF}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.depth_ofCNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula, FABL.DepthCircuit.depth, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and every conjunctive normal form formula on $n$ variables,
the depth of its associated circuit is $2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Size of the circuit representing a CNF]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.size_ofCNF}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.size_ofCNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula, FABL.CNFFormula.size, FABL.CircuitTail.internalNodeCount, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.size}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\psi$ be a CNF formula on $n$ Boolean variables. The circuit formed from $\psi$ by
using its clauses as the first layer and a single output layer has size equal to the
number of clauses in $\psi$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $\psi$ be a conjunctive normal form on $n$
coordinates, with clauses given by terms of pairwise distinct literal coordinates. The
width of the circuit formed from these clauses as its first layer of OR gates equals the
width of $\psi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the CNF circuit]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofCNF}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofCNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula, FABL.CNFFormula.clauseEval, FABL.CNFFormula.eval, FABL.CircuitGate.evalTerm, FABL.CircuitTail.eval, FABL.DepthCircuit.eval, FABL.DepthCircuit.evalLayer1, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $n$, every CNF formula on $n$ variables, and every sign vector
$x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the associated circuit evaluates at $x$ to the same sign as the
formula.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Circuit representation of a CNF function]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction_ofCNF}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction_ofCNF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CNFFormula, FABL.CNFFormula.toBooleanFunction, FABL.DepthCircuit.eval_ofCNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.ofCNF, FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction}
\difficulty{3}
For every CNF formula on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, the Boolean function computed by
the circuit formed from that formula is equal to the function represented by the
formula.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Depth circuit representation]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.HasDepthCircuit}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b007}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch13-circuit-lowerbounds}{pdf-52929dbaa962-p001-b003}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p103-b002}
\statementsource{goldreich-approximation-method}{pdf-988dc9f0ae91-p004-b004}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.HasDepthCircuit}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.DepthCircuit, FABL.DepthCircuit.depth, FABL.DepthCircuit.size, FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction, FABL.DepthCircuit.width}
A Boolean function on $n$ variables has a depth circuit of depth $d$, size at most $s$,
and width at most $w$ if there is a depth circuit with those bounds whose associated
Boolean function is the given function.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A circuit computes its represented function]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.hasDepthCircuit_toBooleanFunction}
\label{FABL.DepthCircuit.hasDepthCircuit_toBooleanFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DepthCircuit, FABL.DepthCircuit.HasDepthCircuit, FABL.DepthCircuit.depth, FABL.DepthCircuit.size, FABL.DepthCircuit.toBooleanFunction, FABL.DepthCircuit.width}
\difficulty{1}
Every layered circuit $C$ computes its associated Boolean function and therefore
witnesses that this function has a circuit representation with depth equal to the depth
of $C$, size equal to the size of $C$, and first-layer width equal to the width of $C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Circuit representation of a DNF]
\lean{FABL.DepthCircuit.hasDepthCircuit_ofDNF}

\difficulty{1}
Every DNF formula on $n$ variables is computed by a layered circuit of depth $2$, whose
size is the number of terms in the formula and whose first-layer width is the maximum
